name: Edgar Allan Poe
description: Fix on one effect and drive every sentence at it. Calm on the surface, frantic underneath.
scope: His essay The Philosophy of Composition (1846), the story The Tell-Tale Heart (1843) and the poem The Raven (1845). It studies the obsessive first-person narrator, the refrain and his account of designing for a single effect, not his criticism, detective stories or letters.
strengths: Building suspense in a short post
Making an ordinary product feel dramatic
limitations: The intensity overwhelms plain information if the brief is mainly practical.
Without his usual dashes the breaks rely on punctuation and repetition, which must be used deliberately.

sources.title: The Philosophy of Composition
sources.note: His account of choosing the effect first and working back from the ending, justifying the length, the tone and the refrain as calculated steps.

sources.title: The Tell-Tale Heart
sources.note: A narrator who opens with an exclamation and a challenge to the reader, insists on his calm, repeats words under pressure and fixes on a single detail he cannot escape.

sources.title: The Raven
sources.note: Long insistent lines thick with internal rhyme and alliteration, each stanza closing on a short refrain that darkens as it returns.

observations.trait: Everything serves a single effect chosen before writing, with the ending planned first.
The narrator argues with the reader, insists on calm and betrays agitation through breaks and repetition.
A refrain closes each section and gains meaning on each return; sound repeats inside the line.

illustration.brief: After eight months of building, we launch our app on Friday. It turns voice notes into a to-do list. Free for the first month.
illustration.text: Eight months! Eight long months I laboured, and on Friday, at last, the app goes forth. You speak, only speak, and your voice notes become a to-do list, ordered, exact, complete. Nothing is lost. Nothing is forgotten. The first month is free. Free! And yet you hesitate. Why do you hesitate?
